core: working definition of a low-fidelity prototype: a rough, quickly made representation of a design that tests ideas before code — synthesized from NN/g's prototype-as-hypothesis framing and IxDF's definition of prototypes as early models
what low fidelity looks like: paper sketches, simple clickable flows, and placeholder content (each named)
why low fidelity first: speed — test the idea while it is cheap to change; grounded in NN/g's 'ripping up a prototype is cheap' argument, Nielsen's early-vs-late estimates, and IxDF's cost framing
what low fidelity is good for: layout, flow, and structure — testing these early
what low fidelity is NOT good for: visual polish, exact spacing, and real content (the named limits)
low fidelity vs high fidelity: rough vs refined — the distinction, with high-fidelity-prototypes referenced as a sibling topic only
honest framing: fidelity should match the question — test structure with rough, test polish with refined
supporting: a user interface prototype is a hypothesis — a candidate design solution — and the straightforward way to test it is to watch users work with it (NN/g)
fidelity refers to how closely a prototype matches the look-and-feel of the final system, varying across interactivity, visuals, and content and commands (NN/g)
the paper-prototype 'computer': a person who knows the design presents the next page when the user interacts with a paper screen (NN/g)
Nielsen's rough estimates: early usability data is about ten times more valuable than late data, and changes are about 100 times cheaper before code is written than after implementation (NN/g)
low-fidelity benefits beyond cost: less pressure on users, designers feel less wedded to the design, stakeholders recognize the work is unfinished (NN/g)
low-fidelity prototypes are fast, cheap, disposable, producible by anyone, and visibly not finalized, which encourages design thinking (IxDF)

claims.claim: A low-fidelity prototype is a rough, quickly made representation of a design that tests ideas before code is written; prototypes in general are early models of a product created to test concepts, gather feedback, and iterate before the final product is developed.
A user interface prototype is a hypothesis — a candidate design solution for a specific design problem — and the most straightforward way to test that hypothesis is to watch users work with it.
Fidelity refers to how closely a prototype matches the look-and-feel of the final system, and it can vary across three areas: interactivity, visuals, and content and commands.
Low-fidelity prototypes are fast and cheap to create, disposable, easy to change between iterations, and producible by anyone; classic examples include paper prototypes and sketches.
It is much cheaper to change a design early: ripping up a prototype is cheap while ripping up code is expensive, and changes become increasingly costly as a project progresses.

Low-fidelity prototypes are best for early-stage concept exploration and initial feedback on basic functionality and flow — layout, flow, and structure — and are not suited to judging visual polish, exact spacing, or real content.
In a paper prototype test, a person who knows the design plays the part of the 'computer,' presenting the next page when the user interacts with a paper screen.
Low-fidelity prototypes put less pressure on users, make designers feel less attached to the design, and signal to stakeholders that the work is not finished.

The fidelity of a prototype should match the question being tested: teams choose a fidelity level appropriate to their goals and stage of development, so rough prototypes test structure and refined prototypes test polish.

conflictingEvidence: Sources agree on the core claims; the tension is definitional, not factual. IxDF lists paper prototypes, sketches, and wireframes as low-fidelity examples and places clickable wireframes at mid-fidelity, while NN/g treats interactivity as one of three independent fidelity dimensions (interactivity, visuals, content), so a rough-sketch flow with working links is low fidelity in visuals and content even if it is high fidelity in interactivity. This lesson therefore treats 'simple clickable flows' as one low-fidelity form when the visuals and content stay rough. IxDF also flags the honest limits of low fidelity — lack of realism can make feedback harder to interpret, results from early versions may be hard to apply to the final product, and the lack of interactivity requires users to imagine parts of the experience — which this lesson presents as the named limits, not as contradictions.

sourceRecords.title: UX Prototypes: Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Defines a user interface prototype as a hypothesis — a candidate design solution; defines fidelity as how closely a prototype matches the look-and-feel of the final system across interactivity, visuals, and content and commands; describes the paper-prototype 'computer' method; details the benefits of low-fidelity prototypes (less preparation time, easy mid-test changes, less pressure on users, designers less wedded to the design, stakeholders see the work as unfinished); argues testing final products is uninformed and risky.

sourceRecords.title: Paper Prototyping: Getting User Data Before You Code
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Jakob Nielsen, April 2003. Paper prototyping lets teams user-test early design ideas at extremely low cost and fix usability problems before wasting money implementing something that does not work; early usability data is roughly ten times more valuable than late data, and changes are roughly 100 times cheaper before code is written than after implementation.

sourceRecords.title: What is a Prototype?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl 2026-08-21. Defines prototypes as early models of a product that simulate its design and functionality, created to test concepts, gather feedback, and iterate before the final product is developed; characterizes low-fidelity prototypes as basic, often hand-drawn representations focused on the core concept and user journey rather than visual details, with pros (fast, cheap, disposable, easy to change, anyone can produce them) and cons (lack of realism, hard to apply results, lack of interactivity, oversimplification); advises choosing the fidelity level appropriate to goals and stage of development; includes the Tim Brown quote 'They slow us down to speed us up.'
